chapter: Cab Calloway's band, Hadacol and closing reflections
title: Danny's gigs, the Fairview Baptist church band and traditional New Orleans music
summary: Danny teaches kids traditional music with Lucien and Charlie Barbarin at Fairview Baptist, says Dixieland was a name whites gave to New Orleans music, and notes musicians play until they die.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: What are you into now, Danny? What are you doing now? -- just to wind this up.
Oh, I'm around. I'm playing some gigs. I play some parties for people. I do that, and I get a little ...(?)...
Well, I know you were telling me yesterday that you went down to try to see the Mayor about an old firehouse or something.

Yeah. I have some kids I've been working with the last nine years. The Fairview Baptist Church Christian(?) Band, which is kids who are musically inclined, and Lucien and me and Charlie Barbarin, we have two sons... That's mostly why I got involved with it. Lucien and Charlie Barbarin, we were teaching them traditional music, which was the beginning -- some people call it Dixieland here, but I don't know what "Dixieland" is. But we call it "traditional New Orleans music," the music that Armstrong, Bechet and Dodds and Noone and Barbarin and all these people learned. It was Dixieland. It was New Orleans music, that later on got the tag.

Yes. It got the tag Dixieland by some Whites. Well, I'm around here, and I still play. Because you play until you die here. That's a tradition here. This is one of the few places where you can go and get a band of seven or ten or twelve people, and everybody is over eighty
years old -- and still can play.
See, we're still around. You can get an old band, I mean, an ancient band, and play... When you take the instruments from the chest, they...
They become alive. And that's what we try to do. Charlie passed away a month or so ago, and I'm playing...
